source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 30 (PDF 202-216, printed 199-213); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 30 (Spectroscopy-2 NMR), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 In chemistry, NMR spectroscopy is particularly used for:

options.text: measuring the boiling points of liquids
identifying organic compounds and determining their structures
separating the components of a mixture

blocks.explanation: In chemistry NMR is particularly used to identify organic compounds and determine their structures (introduction).

book_ref.quote: this technique is particularly used for the identification of organic compounds

blocks.prompt: 2 The two most commonly used NMR methods for organic compounds are:
blocks.explanation: Proton (¹H) NMR and carbon-13 (¹³C) NMR are the two most commonly used methods (introduction).

book_ref.quote: Proton (¹H) NMR and carbon-13 (¹³C) NMR are two most commonly used methods

blocks.prompt: 3 Which of the following is NOT listed in the chapter as a field where NMR is used?

options.text: study of proteins and natural products

blocks.explanation: NMR is used in chemistry, the polymer industry, the study of proteins and natural products, environment monitoring and the medical field; smelting is not mentioned.

book_ref.quote: polymer industry, study of proteins and natural products, environment monitoring, and medical field

blocks.prompt: 4 NMR spectroscopy is based on which property of nuclei?
blocks.explanation: NMR spectroscopy is based on the magnetic properties (nuclear spin) of nuclei (30.1).

book_ref.quote: NMR spectroscopy is based on the magnetic properties (nuclear spin) of nuclei

blocks.prompt: 5 Which atoms usually show signals in NMR?

options.text: atoms with even mass and even atomic numbers

blocks.explanation: Atoms with odd mass numbers, such as ¹H and ¹³C, usually show NMR signals; their nuclei behave like tiny magnets (30.1).

book_ref.quote: Atoms with odd mass numbers usually show signals on NMR

blocks.prompt: 6 In the absence of a magnetic field, the nuclei of a sample:

options.text: are all aligned with one another
are in two different energy states
are randomly oriented and have the same energy
are all in the high energy state

blocks.explanation: Without a magnetic field all the nuclei have random orientation and the same energy (30.1).

book_ref.quote: In the absence of a magnetic field, all the nuclei have random orientation

blocks.prompt: 7 When placed in a strong magnetic field, nuclei such as ¹H give rise to:

options.text: two spin states, a low energy and a high energy state
three spin states of equal energy

blocks.explanation: In a strong field the nuclei align either with or against the field, giving two spin states: low energy and high energy (30.1, Figure 30.1).

book_ref.quote: these nuclei align themselves either with or against the field

blocks.prompt: 8 The radiation used to flip nuclei from the low to the high energy state in NMR is:
blocks.explanation: By irradiating with radio waves, nuclei in the low energy state absorb energy and move to the higher state (spin flipping) (30.1).

book_ref.quote: By irradiating with radio waves, the nuclei at low energy state can absorb energy

blocks.prompt: 9 The movement of a nucleus from the low energy spin state to the high energy spin state is called:
blocks.explanation: Absorption of radio-wave energy moves the nucleus to the higher energy state; this is spin flipping (30.1).

book_ref.quote: and move to higher energy state (spin flipping)

blocks.prompt: 10 An NMR spectrum is obtained from the energy that nuclei:

options.text: lose as heat to the solvent
emit when they return to their original states

blocks.explanation: When the flipped nuclei return to their original states they emit energy, which is detected and converted into an NMR spectrum (30.1).

book_ref.quote: they emit energy which is detected and converted into an NMR spectrum

blocks.prompt: 11 The position of a nucleus in a compound together with its surrounding atoms is collectively called the:
blocks.explanation: The exact energy to flip a nucleus depends on its position and surrounding atoms, collectively known as the molecular environment (30.1).

book_ref.quote: collectively known as the molecular environment

blocks.prompt: 12 In methanol (CH₃OH), the methyl and hydroxyl hydrogens absorb different frequencies of radio waves because they:
blocks.explanation: The -CH₃ hydrogens (on carbon) and the O-H hydrogen (on oxygen) lie in different environments, so they absorb different amounts of energy (30.1).

book_ref.quote: three hydrogen atoms are attached to a carbon atom and one hydrogen atom is bonded to an oxygen atom

blocks.prompt: 13 Nuclei in different environments can be flipped with radio waves of the same frequency if:

options.text: the strength of the magnetic field is varied
the solvent is changed to water
the magnetic field is switched off

blocks.explanation: Nuclei in different environments can be flipped by radio waves of the same frequency if the magnetic field strength is varied (30.1).

book_ref.quote: Nuclei lying in different environments can be flipped by using the radio waves of same frequency

blocks.prompt: 14 ¹²C nuclei have no net magnetic field because:

options.text: they have an odd mass number
their protons pair their spins and their neutrons pair theirs

blocks.explanation: In nuclei with even atomic and even mass numbers the protons pair their spins and the neutrons pair theirs, so there is no net magnetic field (30.1, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: so such nuclei, e.g. ¹²C, have no net magnetic field

blocks.prompt: 15 Which statement about nuclei with even atomic and even mass numbers is correct?

options.text: they always have equal numbers of protons and neutrons
they have even numbers of protons and neutrons, not always equal
they always give strong NMR signals
they have an odd number of neutrons

blocks.explanation: Such nuclei have an even number of protons and an even number of neutrons but not always equal numbers, e.g. ¹⁸O has 8 protons and 10 neutrons (30.1, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: but not always equal numbers (¹⁸O has 8 protons and 10 neutrons)

blocks.prompt: 16 Ordinary solvents are avoided in ¹H NMR because they:

options.text: contain hydrogen atoms that give strong interfering signals

blocks.explanation: Ordinary solvents contain hydrogen atoms which produce strong signals and interfere with the spectrum of the sample (30.2).

book_ref.quote: Ordinary solvents contain hydrogen atoms which produce strong signals

blocks.prompt: 17 Which of the following is a deuterated solvent used in ¹H NMR?
blocks.explanation: Deuterated solvents such as CDCl₃ and CD₃OD (deuterated methanol) are used (30.2).

book_ref.quote: deuterated solvents such as CDCl₃ (deuterated chloroform) or CD₃OD (deuterated methanol)

blocks.prompt: 18 If ordinary CHCl₃ were used as the solvent, the signal of its proton would:

options.text: mask the weaker signals of the sample's protons
appear at 0.0 ppm as the reference
split every peak of the sample

blocks.explanation: Because the solvent is in excess, its single proton's signal would be intense enough to overlap and mask the weaker sample signals (30.2).

book_ref.quote: the signal from its single proton (¹H) would be intense enough to completely overlap

blocks.prompt: 19 In CDCl₃ the hydrogen atom is replaced by:
blocks.explanation: In CDCl₃ hydrogen is replaced by its isotope deuterium (D) (30.2).

book_ref.quote: In CDCl₃, hydrogen (H) is replaced with its isotope Deuterium (D)

blocks.prompt: 20 A deuterated solvent is described as 'silent' in ¹H NMR because deuterium:

options.text: needs a different radio frequency for flipping, so it gives no ¹H peak
absorbs the same frequency as ¹H but more strongly

blocks.explanation: Deuterium requires a different frequency of radio waves for flipping, so it neither absorbs the frequency given to the sample nor shows a ¹H peak (30.2).

book_ref.quote: This makes the solvent "silent", and only the signals of the sample are observed

blocks.prompt: 21 Chemical shift represents the position of a signal relative to:

options.text: the largest peak in the spectrum

blocks.explanation: Chemical shift represents the position of a signal relative to a reference compound (30.3).

book_ref.quote: represents the position of a signal relative to a reference compound

blocks.prompt: 22 The standard reference compound in ¹H NMR is:
blocks.explanation: Tetramethylsilane, Si(CH₃)₄ (TMS), is the standard reference (30.3).

book_ref.quote: Tetramethylsilane, Si(CH₃)₄ (commonly known as TMS) is used as the standard reference

blocks.prompt: 23 The signal of TMS is assigned a chemical shift of:
blocks.explanation: The TMS signal is assigned 0.0 ppm and all other signals are measured from this zero point (30.3).

book_ref.quote: its signal is assigned a value of 0.0 ppm

blocks.prompt: 24 Chemical shift (δ) is measured in:
blocks.explanation: The position of a peak relative to TMS is the chemical shift (δ), measured in parts per million (ppm) (30.3).

book_ref.quote: is called the chemical shift (δ) which is measured in parts per million (ppm) unit

blocks.prompt: 25 How many protons of TMS share the same chemical environment?
blocks.explanation: All 12 protons of TMS (four CH₃ groups) have the same environment and give a single sharp peak (30.3, Did You Know).

book_ref.quote: because all 12 of its protons have the same chemical environment and produce a single sharp peak

blocks.prompt: 26 The protons of TMS appear at the extreme right of the spectrum because of:

options.text: the presence of oxygen in TMS

blocks.explanation: Due to the low electronegativity of silicon, TMS protons appear at the extreme right and do not overlap most organic signals (30.3).

book_ref.quote: (due to the low electronegativity of silicon)

blocks.prompt: 27 TMS is easy to remove after use because it is:

options.text: a solid with a high melting point

blocks.explanation: TMS is chemically inert and volatile, which makes it easy to remove after use (30.3).

book_ref.quote: TMS is chemically inert and volatile, which makes it easy to remove after use

blocks.prompt: 28 In the ¹H NMR spectrum of methanol, the -CH₃ protons appear at:
blocks.explanation: The methyl hydrogens of methanol appear at 3.35 ppm and the O-H hydrogen at 4.80 ppm (30.3, Figure 30.2).

book_ref.quote: the relative position of peak for methyl (-CH₃) hydrogens at 3.35 ppm

blocks.prompt: 29 The O-H proton of methanol appears at a higher δ (4.80 ppm) than the -CH₃ protons because:

options.text: it has a higher electron density around it
it is next to electronegative oxygen, which lowers the electron density around it

blocks.explanation: Protons near electronegative atoms have low electron density and appear at high δ; the O-H proton is next to oxygen (30.3).

book_ref.quote: O-H hydrogen of methanol has a chemical shift of 4.80 ppm

blocks.prompt: 30 Chemically equivalent protons in a molecule:
blocks.explanation: Protons in chemically identical environments are chemically equivalent and show the same chemical shift (30.3).

book_ref.quote: they exhibit the same chemical shift in the ¹H NMR spectra of that molecule

blocks.prompt: 31 Which of the following gives only ONE peak in its ¹H NMR spectrum?
blocks.explanation: All the protons in TMS, methane, ethane, benzene and propanone are chemically equivalent, so each gives a single peak (30.3).

book_ref.quote: All the protons in TMS, methane, ethane, benzene and propanone (acetone) are chemically equivalent

blocks.prompt: 32 Propanone (acetone) gives a single ¹H NMR peak because:

options.text: it has only one hydrogen atom
its protons are exchanged by D₂O
all its protons are chemically equivalent
its C=O group absorbs all the radio waves

blocks.explanation: All six protons of propanone are chemically equivalent, so it gives one absorption peak (30.3).

book_ref.quote: Each of these compounds gives rise to a single absorption peak in its ¹H NMR spectrum

blocks.prompt: 33 How many different proton environments are present in ethanol (C₂H₅OH)?
blocks.explanation: In ethanol a -CH₃ proton differs from a -CH₂- proton and from the O-H proton: three environments (30.3).

book_ref.quote: a proton on a -CH₃ group is different from the one on -CH₂- and O-H in ethanol

blocks.prompt: 34 Protons surrounded by high electron density, as in alkyl groups, have:
blocks.explanation: High electron density (alkyl groups) gives lower δ; low electron density (near F, O, N, Cl) gives higher δ (30.3).

book_ref.quote: Protons surrounded by high electron density (alkyl groups) have lower chemical shift values

blocks.prompt: 35 Protons that lie near electronegative atoms such as F, O, N or Cl appear at:
blocks.explanation: Protons with low electron density, near electronegative atoms like F, O, N, Cl, appear at high δ (30.3).

book_ref.quote: (near electronegative atoms like F, O, N, Cl etc.) appear at high chemical shift values

blocks.prompt: 36 The usual chemical shift range of a ¹H NMR spectrum stated in the chapter is:
blocks.explanation: A ¹H NMR spectrum has a δ range of 0 – 12 ppm; ¹³C NMR has 0 – 220 ppm (30.3, 30.7).

book_ref.quote: A ¹H NMR spectrum has a chemical shift (δ) range of 0 – 12 ppm

blocks.prompt: 37 According to Table 30.1, the protons of CH₃–Ar (alkyl next to an aromatic ring) appear in the range:
blocks.explanation: Table 30.1: alkyl next to an aromatic ring (CH₃–Ar, –CH₂–Ar, >CH–Ar) 2.3 – 3.0 ppm.

book_ref.quote: Alkyl next to aromatic ring

blocks.prompt: 38 Protons attached directly to an aromatic ring (Ar–H) appear in the range:
blocks.explanation: Table 30.1: aromatic protons Ar–H 6.5 – 9.0 ppm.

book_ref.quote: Aromatic (attached to aromatic ring)

blocks.prompt: 39 Vinylic protons of alkenes (>C=CHR) appear in the range:
blocks.explanation: Table 30.1: vinylic (alkene) protons 4.5 – 6.0 ppm.

book_ref.quote: Table 30.1 Chemical shifts of some common types of protons

blocks.prompt: 40 A CH₃ group next to a C=O group (as in a ketone or ester) gives a signal in the range:
blocks.explanation: Table 30.1: alkyl next to C=O (ketone/ester) 2.0 – 2.6 ppm.

book_ref.quote: CH₃–C=O, –CH₂–C=O, >CH–C=O

blocks.prompt: 41 In which range do the protons of a CH₃–O group appear (Table 30.1)?
blocks.explanation: Table 30.1: alkyl next to an electronegative atom (CH₃–O, –CH₂–O, CH₃–Cl, –CH₂–Cl) 3.0 – 4.5 ppm.

book_ref.quote: CH₃–O, –CH₂–O, CH₃–Cl, –CH₂–Cl

blocks.prompt: 42 A singlet at 11.5 ppm in a ¹H NMR spectrum most likely belongs to the proton of:

options.text: an alkyl group next to C=O

blocks.explanation: Table 30.1: carboxylic acid RCOOH 9.0 – 13.0 ppm; 11.5 ppm lies only in this range among the options.

book_ref.quote: Table 30.1 Chemical shifts of some common types of protons

blocks.prompt: 43 The aldehyde proton (RCHO) appears in the range:
blocks.explanation: Table 30.1: aldehyde RCHO 9.0 – 10.0 ppm.

book_ref.quote: Table 30.1 Chemical shifts of some common types of protons

blocks.prompt: 44 According to Table 30.1, the Ar–OH proton of a phenol appears in the range:
blocks.explanation: Table 30.1: phenol Ar–OH 4.5 – 7.0 ppm.

book_ref.quote: Table 30.1 Chemical shifts of some common types of protons

blocks.prompt: 45 Which type of proton has the widest range in Table 30.1, 5.0 – 12.0 ppm?
blocks.explanation: Table 30.1: amide RCONHR 5.0 – 12.0 ppm; alkyl amine 1.0 – 5.0, aryl amine 3.0 – 6.0, aldehyde 9.0 – 10.0 ppm.

book_ref.quote: Table 30.1 Chemical shifts of some common types of protons

blocks.prompt: 46 Protons of an alkane (–CH₃, –CH₂–, >CH–) appear in the range:
blocks.explanation: Table 30.1: alkyl (alkanes) 0.5 – 1.5 ppm, the lowest δ because of high electron density.

book_ref.quote: Table 30.1 Chemical shifts of some common types of protons

blocks.prompt: 47 Which of the following is NOT one of the three pieces of information given by a low-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum?

options.text: the number of different proton environments
the molar mass of the compound
the relative number of protons in each environment

blocks.explanation: A low-resolution spectrum gives the number of different proton environments, their types and the relative number of protons in each (30.4.1).

book_ref.quote: three main pieces of information about the structure of a compound

blocks.prompt: 48 The number of peaks in a ¹H NMR spectrum corresponds to the number of:
blocks.explanation: The number of peaks equals the number of different proton environments, not the number of protons (30.4.1; Book correction in 30.6).

book_ref.quote: corresponds to the number of different chemical environments for protons present in the molecule

blocks.prompt: 49 The chemical shift of a peak tells us the:

options.text: type of chemical environment of the protons

blocks.explanation: The chemical shift of each peak corresponds to the type of chemical environment of the protons giving that peak (30.4.1).

book_ref.quote: corresponds to the type of chemical environment of protons giving rise to that peak

blocks.prompt: 50 The area under a peak in a ¹H NMR spectrum is proportional to the:

options.text: number of protons on the adjacent carbon
number of protons giving that peak

blocks.explanation: The area under each peak is proportional to the number of protons giving rise to it (30.4.1).

book_ref.quote: The area under each peak is proportional to the number of protons giving rise to that peak

blocks.prompt: 51 In the low-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of ethanol (Figure 30.4), the peak at 3.7 ppm is due to:
blocks.explanation: In Figure 30.4, 5.4 ppm is OH, 3.7 ppm is –CH₂– next to oxygen and 1.2 ppm is –CH₃ (30.4.1).

book_ref.quote: The peak having chemical shift 3.7 ppm can be identified as –CH₂– next to oxygen

blocks.prompt: 52 In the ¹H NMR spectrum of ethanol, the signal at 1.2 ppm belongs to the:
blocks.explanation: The signal at 1.2 ppm is identified as the methyl group (–CH₃ protons) of ethanol (30.4.1).

book_ref.quote: while the signal at 1.2 ppm can be identified as methyl group

blocks.prompt: 53 The relative peak areas in the ¹H NMR spectrum of ethanol (OH : CH₂ : CH₃) are:
blocks.explanation: The peaks are labelled 1H, 2H and 3H: relative areas 1 : 2 : 3 for OH, CH₂ and CH₃ (30.4.1).

book_ref.quote: peaks are labeled 1H, 2H and 3H to show relative peak areas in 1:2:3 ratio

blocks.prompt: 54 A compound gives three ¹H NMR peaks with relative areas 3 : 2 : 3 and the simplest whole-number ratio equals the actual numbers. The total number of hydrogen atoms in the molecule is:
blocks.explanation: The sum of the protons in each environment gives the total: 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 hydrogen atoms (method of 30.4.1).

book_ref.quote: Hence, there are total 6 hydrogen (1+2+3) atoms in an ethanol molecule

blocks.prompt: 55 A compound C₂H₄O₂ shows two ¹H NMR peaks with relative areas 2.4 : 0.8. How many protons does each peak represent?
blocks.explanation: 2.4 : 0.8 = 3 : 1; total 4 H, so the peaks represent 3 H and 1 H (30.4.1).

book_ref.quote: This ratio matches with the number of protons in each environment

blocks.prompt: 56 A low-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of a compound shows four peaks. This means the molecule has:
blocks.explanation: Each peak stands for a different chemical environment; four peaks mean four proton environments (30.4.1).

book_ref.quote: The spectrum has three peaks which shows that there are three different proton environments

blocks.text: 30.4.2 High-Resolution 1H NMR and Splitting of Peaks

blocks.prompt: 57 Besides nearby electrons, the NMR signal of a proton is affected by:
blocks.explanation: NMR signals are affected by nearby electrons and also by protons on adjacent atoms; this is seen in high resolution (30.4.2).

book_ref.quote: but also by protons on the adjacent atoms

blocks.prompt: 58 In a high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum, a peak is often found to be made up of:
blocks.explanation: High resolution reveals that each peak is often a cluster of sub-peaks, due to splitting by protons on adjacent carbons (30.4.2).

book_ref.quote: it reveals that each peak is often made up of a cluster of sub-peaks

blocks.prompt: 59 According to the n+1 rule, n stands for the number of:

options.text: protons on the adjacent carbon atom(s)

blocks.explanation: A signal splits into n+1 sub-peaks, where n is the number of protons on the adjacent carbon atoms (30.4.2).

book_ref.quote: A signal usually splits into n+1 sub-peaks, where n is the number of protons on adjacent carbon atoms

blocks.prompt: 60 In the high-resolution spectrum of ethanol, the -CH₃ signal is a:
blocks.explanation: The adjacent carbon carries 2 protons, so 2 + 1 = 3 sub-peaks: a triplet (30.4.2).

book_ref.quote: the -CH₃ peak is split into three sub-peaks (known as triplet)

blocks.prompt: 61 The -CH₂- signal of ethanol splits into four sub-peaks because the adjacent carbon carries:
blocks.explanation: There are 3 protons on the adjacent carbon, so 3 + 1 = 4 sub-peaks: a quartet (30.4.2).

book_ref.quote: -CH₂- peak is split into four sub-peaks (known as a quartet)

blocks.prompt: 62 The -OH signal of ethanol is not split because its hydrogen is:

options.text: bonded to an oxygen atom instead of a carbon atom

blocks.explanation: The -OH signal is not split because its hydrogen is bonded to oxygen instead of carbon (30.4.2).

book_ref.quote: The -OH signal is not split because hydrogen is bonded to an oxygen atom instead of carbon atom

blocks.prompt: 63 The ¹H NMR peak of ethane (CH₃-CH₃) is not split even though each carbon has 3 neighbouring protons, because:

options.text: all its protons are chemically equivalent

blocks.explanation: Chemically equivalent protons do not cause splitting of each other; all the hydrogens of ethane are equivalent (30.4.2, Figure 30.6).

book_ref.quote: chemically equivalent protons do not cause splitting of their neighbouring protons

blocks.prompt: 64 -OH and -NH protons usually appear in a ¹H NMR spectrum as:
blocks.explanation: -OH and -NH protons usually do not show splitting, so they appear as a singlet peak (30.4.2).

book_ref.quote: -OH and -NH protons usually do not show splitting, so these appear as singlet peak

blocks.prompt: 65 A proton whose adjacent carbon carries one proton (n = 1) gives a:
blocks.explanation: Table 30.2: n = 1 gives 1 + 1 = 2 sub-peaks, a doublet (d).

book_ref.quote: Common splitting patterns in high-resolution ¹H NMR spectra

blocks.prompt: 66 A peak that appears as a quartet tells us that the number of protons on the adjacent carbon is:
blocks.explanation: Number of sub-peaks = n + 1; for a quartet 4 = n + 1, so n = 3 (Table 30.2).

book_ref.quote: No. of Protons on Adjacent Carbon Atom (n)

blocks.prompt: 67 The abbreviation 's' for a split peak in Table 30.2 stands for a peak with:
blocks.explanation: s = singlet: n = 0, so 0 + 1 = 1 sub-peak (Table 30.2).

book_ref.quote: Number of Sub-Peaks (n+1)

blocks.prompt: 68 In ethanal (CH₃CHO), the CH₃ signal is split by the single proton on the adjacent carbon into a:
blocks.explanation: n = 1 (the CHO proton), so 1 + 1 = 2 sub-peaks: a doublet (n+1 rule, 30.4.2).

book_ref.quote: The splitting of signals into multiple peaks (e.g., doublets, triplets, quartets)

blocks.prompt: 69 In ethanal (CH₃CHO), the aldehyde proton signal appears as a:
blocks.explanation: The adjacent CH₃ carbon carries 3 protons, so 3 + 1 = 4 sub-peaks: a quartet (n+1 rule, 30.4.2).

book_ref.quote: Number of sub-peaks can be calculated by using 'n+1' rule

blocks.prompt: 70 In methyl ethanoate (CH₃COOCH₃), both ¹H signals appear as singlets because:

options.text: both groups are bonded to oxygen
neither CH₃ group has protons on an adjacent carbon atom

blocks.explanation: One CH₃ is next to the C=O carbon (no H) and the other is next to O; with n = 0, each gives 0 + 1 = 1 sub-peak (30.4.2).

book_ref.quote: This is due to the splitting of each signal due to the presence of protons

blocks.prompt: 71 In 1,1-dichloroethane (CH₃–CHCl₂), the splitting patterns of the CH₃ and CH signals are respectively:
blocks.explanation: CH₃ has 1 neighbouring proton (1 + 1 = 2, doublet); CH has 3 neighbouring protons (3 + 1 = 4, quartet) (n+1 rule).

book_ref.quote: the number of protons (¹H) on the adjacent (neighbouring) carbon atom

blocks.text: 30.4.3 Identifying O-H and N-H Protons by D2O Exchange

blocks.prompt: 72 O-H and N-H protons show a wide range of chemical shift values because they:

options.text: are always equivalent to CH₃ protons

blocks.explanation: The hydrogens of O-H and N-H are easily exchangeable, so their singlet shows a wide range of δ (30.4.3).

book_ref.quote: are easily exchangeable, due to which they show a wide range of chemical shift value

blocks.prompt: 73 The 'D₂O shake' technique is used to detect whether a singlet is due to:

options.text: a CH₃ group next to C=O

blocks.explanation: Deuterium exchange (D₂O shake) detects whether a singlet in the spectrum is due to an O-H or N-H hydrogen (30.4.3).

book_ref.quote: A technique known as 'deuterium exchange' or 'D₂O shake' is used to detect

blocks.prompt: 74 After a few drops of D₂O are added and the tube is shaken, the second ¹H NMR spectrum shows that:

options.text: a new peak appears at 0.0 ppm
the O–H or N–H peak has disappeared
every peak has doubled in area

blocks.explanation: The peak belonging to the O–H or N–H proton disappears in the second spectrum (30.4.3).

book_ref.quote: The peak belonging to O–H or N–H proton disappears in the second spectrum

blocks.prompt: 75 Which protons are easily exchanged with deuterium when D₂O is added?

options.text: protons attached to O or N

blocks.explanation: Protons attached to highly electronegative atoms like O or N are easily exchanged with deuterium (30.4.3).

book_ref.quote: protons (¹H) attached to highly electronegative atoms like O or N are easily exchanged

blocks.prompt: 76 In the exchange R-O-H + D₂O ⇌ R-O-D + HOD, the new O-D group gives:

options.text: no peak in the ¹H NMR spectrum

blocks.explanation: Deuterium needs a different energy for spin flipping than ¹H, so it shows no peak in the ¹H spectrum: it is 'invisible' (30.4.3).

book_ref.quote: it does not show a peak in the ¹H NMR spectrum making it 'invisible'

blocks.prompt: 77 A compound C₂H₄O₂ shows singlets at 2.1 ppm (3H) and 11.4 ppm (1H). After a D₂O shake, the peak that disappears is:
blocks.explanation: The 1H peak at 11.4 ppm (COOH range 9.0 – 13.0) is the O–H proton; it is exchanged with D and disappears. The CH₃ protons are on carbon and stay (30.4.3).

book_ref.quote: A few drops of D₂O are then added to the NMR sample tube

blocks.text: 30.5 Predicting the 1H NMR Spectrum of a Given Molecule

blocks.prompt: 78 The first step in predicting the ¹H NMR spectrum of a molecule is to:
blocks.explanation: Step I: identify the different proton environments; their number = number of peaks expected (30.5).

book_ref.quote: Step I: Identify different proton environments in the molecule.

blocks.prompt: 79 In predicting a ¹H NMR spectrum, the splitting pattern of each peak is found by:
blocks.explanation: Step III: predict the splitting pattern of each peak by applying the n+1 rule (30.5).

book_ref.quote: Step III: Predict the splitting pattern of each peak by applying the 'n+1' rule.

blocks.prompt: 80 Integration ratios in a predicted ¹H spectrum are assigned according to the:

options.text: number of hydrogen atoms in each environment

blocks.explanation: Step IV: assign integration ratios according to the number of hydrogen atoms in each environment (30.5).

book_ref.quote: Step IV: Assign integration ratios according to the number of hydrogen atoms in each environment.

blocks.prompt: 81 If the data table is not available for estimating δ, you should:

options.text: check the nearest bonds and atoms
assume every peak is at 0.0 ppm

blocks.explanation: If the table is not available, check the nearest bonds and atoms: protons near electronegative elements have higher δ, alkyl protons lower (30.5).

book_ref.quote: If the data table is not available, check the nearest bonds and atoms

blocks.prompt: 82 Bromoethane (CH₃-CH₂-Br) is expected to give how many peaks in its ¹H NMR spectrum, with which splitting?

options.text: two peaks: CH₃ quartet and CH₂ triplet
two peaks: CH₃ triplet and CH₂ quartet

blocks.explanation: Like chloroethane (Example 30.1), there are two environments; CH₃ has 2 neighbours (triplet) and CH₂ has 3 neighbours (quartet).

book_ref.quote: Predict the ¹H NMR spectrum of chloroethane (CH₃-CH₂-Cl).

blocks.prompt: 83 In the ¹H NMR spectrum of chloroethane, the ratio of peak areas of -CH₃ to -CH₂- is:
blocks.explanation: -CH₃ has 3 protons and -CH₂- has 2, so the area ratio is 3 : 2 (Example 30.1).

book_ref.quote: Relative peak area: The ratio of peak area for -CH₃ and -CH₂- will be 3:2.

blocks.prompt: 84 In chloroethane, the -CH₂- protons are expected in the range 3.0 – 4.5 ppm because:

options.text: the CH₂ is next to an aromatic ring
the CH₂ is attached to an electronegative chlorine atom
the CH₂ is next to C=O

blocks.explanation: The -CH₂- is attached to an electronegative element, so it shows a higher δ (3.0 – 4.5 ppm); the methyl protons are at 0.5 – 1.5 ppm (Example 30.1).

book_ref.quote: The -CH₂- is attached to an electronegative element, it will show a higher value of chemical shift

blocks.prompt: 85 How many peaks are expected in the ¹H NMR spectrum of methyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₃?
blocks.explanation: Environments: CH₃ of the ethyl part, CH₂ next to C=O and OCH₃: three, so three peaks (Step I, 30.5).

book_ref.quote: one can predict the ¹H NMR spectrum of a given molecule by analyzing its structure

blocks.prompt: 86 In methyl propanoate (CH₃CH₂COOCH₃), the OCH₃ signal is expected to be a:
blocks.explanation: OCH₃ is next to oxygen (3.0 – 4.5 ppm, Table 30.1) and its neighbour O has no protons, so n = 0: singlet.

book_ref.quote: The protons near electronegative elements have higher chemical shift (δ)

blocks.text: 30.6 Determining the Possible Structure of a Molecule from 1H NMR

blocks.prompt: 87 While deducing a structure from a ¹H NMR spectrum, the peak areas give:

options.text: the number of protons in each environment

blocks.explanation: Peak areas give the number of hydrogen atoms in each environment; the number of peaks gives the number of environments (30.6, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: the peak areas give the number of protons in each environment

blocks.prompt: 88 In deducing a structure from ¹H NMR, functional groups are identified from the:
blocks.explanation: Use the chemical shift of each peak, with the data table, to identify functional groups (30.6).

book_ref.quote: Use the chemical shift of each peak to identify functional groups (use data table).

blocks.prompt: 89 A peak in a spectrum is a triplet. The number of protons on the adjacent carbon is:
blocks.explanation: n = number of sub-peaks – 1 = 3 – 1 = 2 (30.6).

book_ref.quote: No. of sub-peaks = n +1; n = No. of sub-peaks – 1

blocks.prompt: 90 The last step in deducing a structure from a ¹H NMR spectrum is to:

options.text: combine all the information to assemble the structure

blocks.explanation: Finally, combine the information from peak count, shifts, areas and splitting to assemble the complete structure (30.6).

book_ref.quote: Combine this information to assemble the complete molecular structure.

blocks.prompt: 91 In Example 30.2, the singlet at 2.2 ppm (3H) of the ester is due to:

options.text: a CH₃ group next to CH₂
a CH₃ group next to C=O
a CH₂ group next to O

blocks.explanation: The 2.2 ppm singlet (3H) is a CH₃ next to C=O; singlet means 1 – 1 = 0 neighbouring protons (Example 30.2).

book_ref.quote: The ¹H NMR spectrum of an ester is given below. Deduce the structure of the ester.

blocks.prompt: 92 In the ester of Example 30.2, the CH₂ signal at 3.9 ppm is a:

options.text: doublet, because it has one neighbouring proton
singlet, because it is next to oxygen
quartet, because it has three neighbouring protons
triplet, because it has two neighbouring protons

blocks.explanation: The CH₂ next to O has the CH₃ group (3 H) as neighbour, so it is a quartet, 4 – 1 = 3 (Example 30.2, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: its signal at 3.9 ppm is a quartet, 4 – 1 = 3, as the spectrum shows

blocks.prompt: 93 The ester deduced in Example 30.2 is:
blocks.explanation: Combining the peaks (CH₃–C=O singlet, O–CH₂ quartet, CH₃–CH₂ triplet) gives H₃C–CO–O–CH₂–CH₃ (Example 30.2).

book_ref.quote: H₃C–CO–O–CH₂–CH₃ (the C=O printed with its O above)

blocks.prompt: 94 A compound C₈H₁₀ shows a triplet at 1.2 ppm (3H), a quartet at 2.6 ppm (2H) and a peak at 7.2 ppm (5H). The compound is:
blocks.explanation: 7.2 ppm (5H) is Ar–H (6.5 – 9.0); 2.6 ppm is –CH₂–Ar (2.3 – 3.0), a quartet next to CH₃; 1.2 ppm is CH₃, a triplet next to CH₂ (Tables 30.1, 30.2).

book_ref.quote: Analyze the splitting pattern and calculate the number of adjacent protons

blocks.prompt: 95 ¹²C is NMR inactive because:

options.text: it has an odd number of neutrons
it has even numbers of protons and neutrons, so no magnetic property

blocks.explanation: The ¹²C nucleus has no magnetic properties because of its even number of protons and neutrons (even mass number), so it is NMR inactive (30.7).

book_ref.quote: The nucleus of ¹²C does not have magnetic properties

blocks.prompt: 96 The ¹³C nucleus possesses magnetic spin because of its:
blocks.explanation: ¹³C has an odd number of neutrons, so it possesses magnetic spin and gives NMR spectra (30.7).

book_ref.quote: the ¹³C nucleus possesses magnetic spin due to its odd number of neutrons

blocks.prompt: 97 The chemical shift range of ¹³C NMR is:
blocks.explanation: ¹³C NMR shifts are measured from TMS (0.0 ppm) and range from 0 – 220 ppm (30.7).

book_ref.quote: However, the ¹³C NMR has a range of chemical shift from 0 – 220 ppm

blocks.prompt: 98 In ¹³C NMR, the solvent CDCl₃ produces a small signal near:
blocks.explanation: The ¹³C signal of CDCl₃ is near 77 ppm (a 1:1:1 triplet centred at 77.16 ppm) (30.7, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: The ¹³C signal of CDCl₃ is near 77 ppm

blocks.prompt: 99 The reference molecule for chemical shifts in ¹³C NMR is:
blocks.explanation: Like ¹H NMR, ¹³C chemical shifts are compared to TMS (δ = 0.0 ppm) (30.7).

book_ref.quote: Like ¹H NMR, chemical shift (δ in ppm) in ¹³C NMR is compared to the reference molecule TMS

blocks.prompt: 100 The environment of a carbon atom is determined by:

options.text: the types of atoms directly attached to it

blocks.explanation: A carbon atom's environment is determined by the types of atoms directly attached to it (30.7.1).

book_ref.quote: A carbon atom's environment is determined by the types of atoms directly attached to it

blocks.prompt: 101 How many different carbon environments are present in 2-methylpropane?
blocks.explanation: The three methyl carbons share one environment and the tertiary carbon has another: two environments (30.7.1).

book_ref.quote: all three methyl carbon atoms in 2-methylpropane have the same environment

blocks.prompt: 102 Chemically non-equivalent carbon atoms in a molecule:

options.text: appear at the same chemical shift
do not appear in the spectrum

blocks.explanation: Carbon atoms in different environments are non-equivalent and appear at different chemical shifts in ¹³C NMR (30.7.1).

book_ref.quote: Carbon atoms in different environments are chemically non-equivalent

blocks.prompt: 103 A ¹³C peak at 205 ppm most likely belongs to a:
blocks.explanation: Table 30.3: carbonyl carbon 190 – 220 ppm; carboxyl 160 – 185, nitrile 100 – 125, alkyl 0 – 50 ppm.

book_ref.quote: Table 30.3 Chemical shifts of different carbon environments

blocks.prompt: 104 The carbon of a –COOH or –COOR group appears in the range:
blocks.explanation: Table 30.3: carboxyl carbon (R–COOH, –COOR), sp², 160 – 185 ppm.

book_ref.quote: Table 30.3 Chemical shifts of different carbon environments

blocks.prompt: 105 Alkene and aryl (benzene ring) carbons appear in the range:
blocks.explanation: Table 30.3: sp² alkene or aryl carbons 110 – 160 ppm.

book_ref.quote: Table 30.3 Chemical shifts of different carbon environments

blocks.prompt: 106 An sp³ carbon atom bonded to oxygen (C–O) appears in the range:
blocks.explanation: Table 30.3: sp³ carbon next to oxygen (C–O) 50 – 70 ppm.

book_ref.quote: Carbon atom next to oxygen

blocks.prompt: 107 The carbon of a nitrile group (R–C≡N) is:
blocks.explanation: Table 30.3: the nitrile carbon R–C≡N is sp hybridized and appears at 100 – 125 ppm.

book_ref.quote: Table 30.3 Chemical shifts of different carbon environments

blocks.prompt: 108 According to Table 30.3, an sp³ carbon bonded to a halogen (C–X) appears at:
blocks.explanation: Table 30.3: carbon atom next to halogen (C–X) 30 – 60 ppm.

book_ref.quote: Carbon atom next to halogen

blocks.prompt: 109 In which of the following molecules are ALL the carbon atoms in the same environment?
blocks.explanation: Both carbon atoms of ethane have the same environment; ethanol, propane and 2-methylpropane each have two carbon environments (30.7.1, 30.7.2).

book_ref.quote: both carbon atoms in ethane have the same environment

blocks.prompt: 110 In a ¹³C NMR spectrum, each peak corresponds to:

options.text: one different environment (type) of carbon atom
one functional group with its hydrogens

blocks.explanation: Each ¹³C peak corresponds to a single, different environment or type of carbon atom (30.7.2).

book_ref.quote: each peak (or signal) corresponds to a single, different environment or type of carbon atom

blocks.prompt: 111 In the ¹³C NMR spectrum of ethanol, the peak near 57 ppm is due to:
blocks.explanation: The peak at 18 ppm is the -CH₃ carbon and the one near 57 ppm is the -CH₂- carbon (C–O range 50 – 70 ppm) (30.7.2).

book_ref.quote: the peak at 18 ppm is for -CH₃ carbon, while the peak near 57 ppm is due to -CH₂- carbon atom

blocks.prompt: 112 Which statement about peak areas in ¹³C NMR is correct?

options.text: they always equal the number of carbon atoms
they give the number of neighbouring protons
they are usually not proportional to the number of carbon atoms
they are always in the ratio 1 : 1

blocks.explanation: Unlike ¹H NMR, relative peak area in ¹³C NMR is usually not proportional to the number of carbon atoms (30.7.2).

book_ref.quote: The relative peak area in ¹³C NMR is usually not proportional to the number of carbon atoms

blocks.prompt: 113 Peaks in a ¹³C NMR spectrum appear as vertical lines because they:
blocks.explanation: The ¹³C peaks do not show splitting, so they appear as vertical lines (30.7.2).

book_ref.quote: Secondly, the peaks do not show splitting, hence these appear as vertical lines

blocks.prompt: 114 How many peaks are expected in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of butane (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃)?
blocks.explanation: The two end CH₃ carbons are equivalent and the two middle CH₂ carbons are equivalent: two environments, two peaks (30.7.2).

book_ref.quote: In propane CH₃ – CH₂ – CH₃, there are two types of carbon environments

blocks.prompt: 115 Propan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂CHOH, is expected to give how many ¹³C NMR peaks?
blocks.explanation: The two CH₃ carbons are equivalent and the CH–OH carbon is different: two carbon environments, two peaks (30.7.2).

book_ref.quote: two peaks are observed in the ¹³C spectrum of ethanol

blocks.prompt: 116 Propanone (CH₃COCH₃) gives two ¹³C peaks. The peak in the range 190 – 220 ppm is due to:
blocks.explanation: The two CH₃ carbons are equivalent (one peak); the carbonyl carbon appears at 190 – 220 ppm (Table 30.3).

book_ref.quote: The ¹³C NMR spectrum is simpler than ¹H NMR

blocks.prompt: 117 Benzene (C₆H₆) is expected to show how many ¹³C NMR peaks, and in which range?

options.text: six peaks, in the range 0 – 50 ppm
one peak, in the range 110 – 160 ppm
one peak, in the range 190 – 220 ppm
two peaks, in the range 160 – 185 ppm

blocks.explanation: All six ring carbons are in the same environment (one peak); aryl carbons appear at 110 – 160 ppm (Table 30.3).

book_ref.quote: Chemical shift of each peak tells about its environment

blocks.text: 30.7.3 Determining the Structure of a Molecule from 13C NMR

blocks.prompt: 118 A compound with 4 carbon atoms shows only 2 peaks in its ¹³C NMR spectrum. This means that:

options.text: there are only two different carbon environments
two carbon atoms give no signal
two peaks are hidden by CDCl₃

blocks.explanation: The number of peaks tells the number of different carbon environments; some carbons are chemically equivalent (30.7.3).

book_ref.quote: The number of peaks in the spectrum tells the number of different types (environments) of carbon atoms

blocks.prompt: 119 The position (ppm value) of a ¹³C peak tells us:

options.text: the number of hydrogen atoms on it
the molar mass of the compound
the kind of compound or group the carbon is present in

blocks.explanation: The ppm value tells whether the carbon is in an alkane, alkene, alkyne, aromatic or carbonyl compound, assigned with Table 30.3 (30.7.3).

book_ref.quote: tells whether the carbon atom is present in an alkane, alkene, alkyne, aromatic or carbonyl compound

blocks.prompt: 120 Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol are each expected to show how many ¹³C NMR peaks?
blocks.explanation: All four carbons in each of these alcohols are in different environments, so each is expected to show 4 peaks (30.7.3).

book_ref.quote: The structure of the unknown compound cannot be butan-1-ol or butan-2-ol

blocks.prompt: 121 A compound C₂H₆O shows only ONE peak in its ¹³C spectrum, in the range 50 – 70 ppm. The compound is:
blocks.explanation: One peak means both carbons are equivalent, and both are bonded to O (50 – 70 ppm): CH₃–O–CH₃. Ethanol gives two peaks (30.7.3).

book_ref.quote: Use the information from the peak count and positions to draw possible structures

blocks.prompt: 122 The ¹³C spectrum of the C₄H₁₀O compound in Figure 30.8 (69.0, 30.5 and 19.0 ppm) actually fits:
blocks.explanation: 2-methoxypropane would give two C–O carbons; the values 69.0, 30.5 and 19.0 ppm fit 2-methylpropan-1-ol, which also has three carbon environments (Book correction, 30.7.3).

book_ref.quote: The values 69.0, 30.5 and 19.0 ppm fit 2-methylpropan-1-ol

blocks.prompt: 123 How many isomers does C₄H₁₀O have in all (alcohols and ethers)?
blocks.explanation: C₄H₁₀O has four alcohols and three ethers: 4 + 3 = 7 isomers (Book correction, 30.7.3).

book_ref.quote: C₄H₁₀O also has more than three isomers (four alcohols and three ethers)
